It used Nnpar 1.0, a non-parametric multivariate sample-size method pooling information across ten correlated outcome scales at rho = 0.4, and such a method can legitimately require fewer subjects than a univariate test. This is therefore a finding that the published power statement cannot be reproduced from the parameters given, not a demonstration that it is arithmetically wrong. findings.plain: Before running a trial, researchers calculate how many patients they need to have a fair chance of detecting a real effect. This study says 30 per group gives it an 80% chance of spotting a moderate difference. Redoing that calculation the two standard ways gives 53 and 64 per group; at 30, the realistic chance is closer to 50%. The authors used specialised software for correlated outcomes that can legitimately justify a smaller number, so this is not proof the figure is wrong -- but as published, the calculation cannot be checked or reproduced. To their credit, the authors say elsewhere in the paper that the study was underpowered.

consequence.explanation: The claim that 30 per group affords 80% power to detect a medium effect cannot be reproduced under any standard univariate reading of the stated parameters.

The Bonferroni relation between P.unadj and P.adj WAS verified for all six non-capped cells.

not_checked.location: Multiplicity correction across the 22 outcome-by-timepoint families (multiplicity_report)
not_checked.reason: TOOL DEFECT, reproduced in this pass on a fully-formed 22-test payload: n_tests = 0 returned. Family-wise error rate, the Bonferroni/Holm/BH/BY thresholds and the surviving-claims interval could not be computed, and no hand arithmetic was substituted. n_claims_lost_to_correction is therefore unknown, not zero.

not_checked.location: Linked replication dataset, duplication analysis under correct column exclusions (detect_raw_duplication)
not_checked.reason: TOOL DEFECT. exclude_columns had no effect when passed as a JSON array or as a comma-separated string; both sweep runs reported n_columns_excluded = 0 and produced byte-identical output. No trustworthy duplication verdict is available for this dataset.

The annex prints only ADJUSTED p-values, not the unadjusted ones, so the P.adj = 3 x P.unadj relation verified for the main tables cannot be checked here. The adjusted values were read and used for interpretation, but the adjustment arithmetic is unverifiable as printed.

Figure extraction was not run and no values were read off the plots. All four figures carry numbers appearing nowhere in the text or tables: per-arm sex counts (Figure 1), age medians and quartiles (Figure 2), and the composite primary endpoint's distribution and notched 95% confidence intervals at both timepoints (Figures 3, 4). The primary endpoint's only interval estimates therefore went unchecked.

GRIM deliberately NOT applied. Age here is continuous, not integer -- the deposited dataset derives it from birth-date and presentation-date columns -- and running GRIM on a continuous measure is the most common route to a false accusation. Independently, the per-arm sample sizes GRIM would need are never reported.

not_checked.location: All p-values in Tables 1 and 2 and Supplementary Annex 1 (GRIM-U rank-sum granularity)
not_checked.reason: Deliberately not applied. GRIM-U is valid only for Mann-Whitney U / Wilcoxon rank-sum p-values with stated group sizes. These are Kruskal-Wallis omnibus and Dunn post-hoc p-values, which use the pooled rank variance across all three groups, so the granularity argument does not hold; applying it here would be the top false-accusation risk for this paper.

statcheck recovered zero statistics, and that is a fact about the reporting FORMAT, not evidence the paper is clean. The paper writes 'Kruskal-Wallis chi-squared = 0.57734, df = 2, p-value = 0.7493' rather than APA inline form, which the parser does not recognise. The automated NHST consistency check contributed nothing to this review.

not_checked.location: Per-arm randomized, ITT and per-protocol sample sizes
not_checked.reason: Never reported for any of the three arms, so percentage-based checks (grim_percentage on per-arm rates, reconstruct_2x2 on the adverse-event distribution across arms) had no denominator and could not be run.

not_checked.location: Secondary outcomes: eye tracking (Tobii Pro TX300) and EEG
not_checked.reason: Collected but explicitly deferred: 'Since these secondary measures require distinct data processing and specialized analysis, they will be reported in subsequent manuscripts.' No statistics are given, so nothing is checkable. Noted because measures collected but never analysed are a reporting pattern worth an editor's attention.

limitations: FIGURES WERE NOT READ. This agent reads text and tables; the optional figure-extraction pass was not run for this paper, and no values were read off any plot. That matters more than usual here: Figures 3 and 4 carry notched 95% confidence intervals for the composite primary endpoint at both timepoints, and those are the ONLY interval estimates anywhere in the paper. Figures 1 and 2 similarly hold the only per-arm sex counts and the only age medians and quartiles.

The strongest forensic check available for a randomized trial -- baseline similarity across arms (Carlisle-Stouffer-Fisher, Table 1 dispersion) -- could not be run at all, because the paper reports no baseline characteristics table and no baseline comparison p-values. This review is therefore silent on the question those methods answer, in both directions: nothing here supports or undermines the randomization.

Two tools failed on our own inputs rather than on the paper. multiplicity_report returned n_tests = 0 for a fully-formed 22-test payload submitted in this pass, so no family-wise error rate, correction threshold or surviving-claims count was computed, and n_claims_lost_to_correction is unknown rather than zero. detect_raw_duplication ignored exclude_columns across both sweep attempts, so its highly_suspicious verdict on the deposited dataset was computed with by-design repeating columns included and has been withdrawn.

The headline finding is a bracketing argument, not a tool computation: no validated tool in this kit converts a chi-squared statistic plus degrees of freedom to a p-value. It rests on the paper's own printed chi-squared/p pairs at df = 2 and on p being strictly decreasing in chi-squared, which is logically necessary but was not verified by an independent engine. That is why it is graded highly_suspicious rather than impossible.

This system reads ONE paper and reaches no network. Two questions a reader needs in order to weight the reporting anomalies here are outside its reach entirely: whether similar discrepancies appear in other papers by the same authors, and how this trial's reporting completeness compares with equivalent trials in traumatic brain injury. The interpretation is therefore partly ours and partly the reader's.

The ISRCTN registration number is absent from the paper, so no pre-specification claim -- including the promised stratified second-line analysis -- could be checked against the registered protocol. Any statement in this review about what was or was not pre-planned rests solely on the paper's own text.

The deposited dataset's column headers were read during the sweep and not re-read at source in this editorial pass, so the duplicated Visit-3 column names are reported at medium rather than high confidence.

checkable.note: Coverage: no table cell in this paper is of a kind any check consumes, so nothing was checkable. This is a statement about the tables, not a clean result.

questions_for_authors.question: The Results give the Day 180 composite cognitive outcome as "χ² = 5.833, p = 0.54", while Supplementary Annex 1 prints p = 0.05752 for χ² = 5.7111 and p = 0.04779 for χ² = 6.082 at the same df = 2. Could you confirm the Day 180 p-value, and state whether 0.54 should read 0.054?
questions_for_authors.why: Settles the headline finding. A one-character correction would resolve it entirely; anything else would indicate the discrepancy is in the analysis rather than the typesetting.

questions_for_authors.question: The Discussion states that "primary outcomes and their subscales did not show statistically significant differences", but Supplementary Annex 1 reports Digit Span Backward at Day 180 with p = 0.02649 (ITT) and p = 0.04779 (PP), and a Bonferroni-adjusted CRB + rTMS versus PLC + SHM contrast of 0.0227401 and 0.0423081 respectively. How should that sentence be read against those values?
questions_for_authors.why: Establishes whether the narrative sentence is an oversight or reflects a deliberate interpretive judgement (for example, discounting the result for multiplicity) that the paper does not currently state.

questions_for_authors.question: Could you provide the number of patients randomized to each of the three arms, the per-arm intention-to-treat and per-protocol sizes, and a baseline characteristics table for the ITT population? The paper gives per-arm counts only for the 64-patient composite subset (PLC + SHM: 24, CRB + SHM: 20, CRB + rTMS: 20).
questions_for_authors.why: Without per-arm denominators neither allocation balance nor differential attrition can be assessed, and the baseline-similarity checks standard for randomized trials cannot be run at all.

questions_for_authors.question: In the deposited dataset (Harvard Dataverse DOFCIV, sheet 'ITT_analysis set'), the Visit-3 column block runs CWTTM1_3, CWTTM2_3, CWTTM3_3, then SCWT_W-D_2 and SCWT_C-D_2, then DGFRES_3, DGBRES_3, so those two names and their z_ companions each appear twice in the header. Do those columns hold Visit-2 or Visit-3 values?
questions_for_authors.why: The Day-180 composite primary endpoint is assembled from these z_ columns; if the values are from Visit 2, the six-month result incorporates two stale measurements.

questions_for_authors.question: The Methods state that "In case of heterogeneities, stratified analyses were performed as second-line analyses", and the Discussion reports that "the Cerebrolysin and sham group was roughly five years older, on average". Were the stratified or age-adjusted analyses performed, and if so could the results be made available?
questions_for_authors.why: The paper pre-specifies an analysis, then reports the condition that triggers it, then reports no such analysis; this determines whether the primary comparison was ever adjusted for the imbalance the authors themselves identify.

questions_for_authors.question: Could you give the ISRCTN registration number, and confirm the amendment history? The Methods list amendments on "171/02.04.2018" and "30/05/2019", while the inclusion criteria record a further change dated 28/02/2020 raising the age limit from 70 to 80 years.
questions_for_authors.why: The registration number is required to verify pre-specification of outcomes and analyses; the first listed amendment date is not well-formed, and the 2020 eligibility change matches neither listed amendment.

questions_for_authors.question: The Methods name three CANTAB subscales (One Touch Stockings of Cambridge, Multitasking Test, Reaction Time) among the ten co-primary instruments, and their columns appear in the deposited dataset at all three visits, but Supplementary Annex 1 reports group differences for the other seven instruments only. Could the individual group-difference analyses for those three be provided?
questions_for_authors.why: These three measures contribute to the composite primary endpoint but have no reported individual analysis, so the claim that individual scales resemble the composite cannot be checked for them.

report_markdown:
This is a phase II, single-centre, three-arm randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 93 patients with moderate-to-severe traumatic brain injury, conducted in Cluj-Napoca between April 2018 and September 2021. It asks whether adding repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation to Cerebrolysin improves cognition beyond Cerebrolysin alone, and beyond placebo. The primary endpoint is a composite z-score of change from baseline across ten neurocognitive instruments, assessed at Day 101 and Day 180 and analysed non-parametrically (Kruskal-Wallis, with Dunn post-hoc tests and Bonferroni adjustment). The authors conclude that the combination is safe and well tolerated, that no primary outcome reached statistical significance, and that descriptive trends favour both active arms.

## What verified

The arithmetic this paper does print is in good order. Every participant-flow relation reconciles exactly: the three composite subgroups sum to 64, the per-arm adverse-event counts sum to the stated 21, the intention-to-treat population plus the seven excluded patients equals the 93 enrolled, the per-protocol population plus the two named losses equals the intention-to-treat set, and the COVID visit delays sum to 16. Every Bonferroni relation in both main tables that is not capped at 1 reproduces at the printed precision, with a largest discrepancy of one part in ten million -- confirming three comparisons per family and that the adjustment was applied as described. Both tables typed at 100% coverage with no ambiguous cells. That is what a carefully prepared results section looks like, and it is worth saying plainly.

It also has to be said what that coverage does not extend to. This paper reports no group means, no standard deviations and no confidence intervals for any outcome -- results appear only as chi-squared values, Dunn Z statistics and p-values. The entire granularity family of checks (GRIM, GRIMMER, DEBIT, SPRITE) therefore has nothing to work on, not because the paper passed them but because it reports no quantity they apply to. Eleven summation relations, one power calculation and thirty-six typed cells is the real extent of what could be recomputed against a paper reporting 291 statistics.

## Why the headline problem is the one it is

Three considerations put the Day-180 p-value first. It sits on a co-primary endpoint, which the safety findings and the reporting gaps do not. It is contradicted by the paper's own supplementary material rather than by any assumption we supplied. And the contradiction is corroborated twice over: the companion Day-101 figure is internally consistent, which rules out a systematic problem with how these tests were run, and Table 2's Day-180 post-hoc contrast of P.unadj = 0.02578002 is simply not compatible with an omnibus p of 0.54.

The likeliest cause is a dropped decimal point, and it should be read that way until the authors say otherwise. It is worth noting that the error runs in the direction of understating the authors' own result -- as does the discrepancy over Digit Span Backward, where the paper denies a significant subscale finding that its annex reports. A paper shading its numbers in its own favour looks different from this.

## Where the reporting, rather than the arithmetic, is the problem

The recurring pattern is that this trial is difficult to check because of what it omits. A three-arm randomised trial reported under CONSORT gives no baseline characteristics table, no per-arm randomised or analysis-population sizes, and no registration number. Twenty-two intention-to-treat patients -- 26% of that population -- are absent from the primary composite analysis, attributed only to "missing data", and cannot be located by arm. Three of ten stated co-primary instruments feed the composite score and are never reported individually. A stratified analysis is pre-specified, its triggering condition is reported in the Discussion, and it never appears.

None of these is an anomaly in the sense of a number that cannot be right. Together they mean that the checks which would ordinarily carry the most weight on a randomised trial -- baseline similarity across arms, per-arm proportion reconstruction, effect-size plausibility against external benchmarks -- had no input at all. That is a hole in this review, not a clean result, and it should not be read as one.

## What remains genuinely unresolved

Two things. Whether the Day-180 figure is a typesetting slip or an error in the analysis itself cannot be settled from the published record; only the authors can say. And whether the two mislabelled Stroop columns in the Visit-3 block of the deposited dataset hold six-month or three-month values matters, because those columns feed the six-month composite -- but the column names alone establish a labelling defect, not duplicated content, and the raw-data scan found no repeated column sequences. Both are one-line answers for the authors and neither presupposes anything went wrong.

The published dataset deserves acknowledgement. Making participant-level data available is what allowed the column-naming problem to be seen at all, and it is more than most trials of this size provide.

Overall: the numbers this paper prints are largely consistent with each other, but several of its stated conclusions are not consistent with its own supplementary material, and too much of the trial is unreported for its central claims to be independently verified. The efficacy and safety conclusions warrant clarification rather than acceptance as they stand.
